summary: This Standards Track document specifies a TLS 1.3 extension that lets a client and server authenticate with certificates while also mixing in an external pre-shared key for the encryption. It obsoletes the Experimental RFC 8773.

eli5.summary: To enter, you show an ID card and also know a secret handshake, and both are used together to make the lock stronger.

questions: why use an external psk with tls 1.3 certificates
does an external psk protect against quantum computers
subtitle: A TLS 1.3 extension that mixes an external pre-shared key into the handshake while keeping certificate authentication.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 normally authenticates with a certificate or with a pre-shared key, not both, and traffic recorded today could be decrypted if a quantum computer breaks the key agreement.
tldr.mechanism: The tls_cert_with_extern_psk extension is an empty flag in the ClientHello and ServerHello that tells both sides to feed an external PSK into the key schedule alongside the (EC)DHE secret, while authentication still uses certificates.
tldr.outcome: A strong external PSK of at least 128 bits protects confidentiality against a future quantum computer, but it does not improve authentication. This RFC obsoletes the Experimental RFC 8773.

facts.label: Minimum PSK size for CRQC protection

today: RFC 9973 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It obsoletes the Experimental RFC 8773, so it is now the definition of this extension, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Certificates Plus a Pre-Shared Key
sections.content:
The TLS 1.3 handshake (RFC 9846) offers two forms of server authentication that exclude each other. The server proves it holds a private key matching a certificate, or it proves it holds a pre-shared key (PSK). A PSK from an earlier handshake is a resumption PSK, and one established by any other means is an external PSK.

RFC 9973 specifies an extension that permits certificate-based authentication and also feeds an external PSK into the TLS 1.3 key schedule.
sections.eli5: Normally you either show an ID card or say a secret password. This lets you do both at once.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
There are two motivations. The first is confidentiality against a future Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC). Such a machine could break the key agreement that TLS 1.3 uses. If a strong external PSK is also in the key schedule, an attacker has to learn the PSK as well as the key-agreement secret to break confidentiality. Here, "strong" means the PSK was generated and distributed so that a CRQC cannot learn it. How that is done is out of scope.

The RFC is clear about the limit: the certificate and signature still authenticate the peer, so authentication cannot be relied on if a CRQC is invented. The PSK does not help there.

The second motivation is initial enrollment of a device in an enterprise network, using a public key together with a factory-provisioned secret value.
sections.eli5: If someone records your secret conversation now, a super-powerful future computer might open it later. A second secret that only you two know keeps the recording locked even then.

sections.title: The Extension and Its Companions
sections.content:
The client sends the tls_cert_with_extern_psk extension in the ClientHello. It must come with key_share, supported_groups, psk_key_exchange_modes and pre_shared_key, and it MUST NOT be sent with early_data. If both arrive, the server MUST end the connection with an illegal_parameter alert. The extension type value is 33, and its body is empty in both the ClientHello and ServerHello.

If the server accepts one of the offered external PSKs, it returns the extension in the ServerHello together with key_share and pre_shared_key. If it accepts none, it leaves the extension out. Receiving the extension in any other message means the handshake MUST be aborted with illegal_parameter.

Clients MUST include the psk_dhe_ke mode and MAY add psk_ke. Servers MUST select psk_dhe_ke on the initial handshake. All PSKs listed MUST be external, and a resumption PSK listed with the extension makes the server abort. The binder for the selected PSK MUST validate, or the server aborts.
sections.eli5: The extension is just a flag that says use our shared secret as well. The client lists the secrets it knows by name, and the server picks one it also knows.

sections.title: Authentication and Key Schedule
sections.content:
Authentication is unchanged. The server proves itself with a signature checked against the public key in its certificate (or a raw public key), using the Certificate and CertificateVerify messages. TLS 1.3 normally forbids a CertificateRequest when a PSK is used. That restriction is lifted when this extension is negotiated, so the client can authenticate with a certificate too.

The key schedule now takes both the external PSK and the (EC)DHE shared secret, so the Early Secret, Handshake Secret and Main Secret all depend on the PSK. If the two sides hold different values for the selected PSK identity, they compute different keys everywhere and the client aborts with a decrypt_error alert. Each external PSK is tied to one hash algorithm, set when the PSK is established, with a default of SHA-256.
sections.eli5: The ID card check works as before. The shared secret is stirred into the lock so that the keys for the conversation can only be made by someone who knows it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The external PSK MUST NOT be the sole basis for authentication. Implementations must protect the PSK, generate it with a secure technique (a weak random number generator can leave little or no security), and make it at least 128 bits. The symmetric key of the chosen ciphersuite also needs to be at least 128 bits. The same content should not be sent over a connection protected with an external PSK and one that is not, because an eavesdropper could correlate them.

The forward secrecy of ephemeral keys is not easily replaced by PSKs. If the PSK is used for one session and known only to client and server, the usual TLS 1.3 properties hold. If it is reused, or known to a group, sessions are not cryptographically separated, and group members could later decrypt recorded traffic of other members with a CRQC.

For privacy, PSK identities travel in plaintext in the ClientHello, so an observer can track clients or servers that reuse an identity. Rotating the identity or using Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849) can reduce this.
sections.eli5: The shared secret has to be long and truly random, and kept safe. If you tell it to a whole club, any member could read recordings of the others later.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 8773
sections.content: The main change is that the document moves from Experimental to Standards Track. It also corrects the order of arguments to HKDF-Extract when an external PSK is present, requires the client to include supported_groups, and expands the motivation to cover CRQC protection and enterprise enrollment. The confidentiality and authentication discussions are now separate, an erratum is corrected, Encrypted Client Hello is covered in the privacy discussion, and terms such as CRQC and Main Secret replace older wording.
sections.eli5: This is the grown-up edition of an older trial version. It fixes a mix-up in how the secrets were stirred together.
